summary: The queue lifecycle flow follows skills/queue.md well: 29 of 35 claims are stated and none is contradicted. The weakest point is the park path: `park --resume` and the `[~]` marker appear in the flow but not in skills/queue.md (only in skills/loop.md and the model script), so the skill doc and the flow disagree on the set of commands and markers. The flow also leaves out the needs-spec failure, the two task modes and the fact that advance verifies nothing itself.

code.overview: This flow is almost entirely code. scripts/queue.ts is the CLI, scripts/queue-model.ts holds the state changes as pure functions, scripts/queue-io.ts stores them in queue.db and re-renders queue.md, and queue-task-origin.ts, queue-claim.ts and queue-delivery.ts carry the add, claim and advance commands. The only part left to the agent is the delivery itself: opening the PR, reading checks and merging, which `queue advance` records but does not verify.

refs.anchor: if (!title) { console.error('usage: queue add "<title>" [--parent <id> | --requested "<human words>"] [flags]'); return 1; }
refs.title: queue add: record one task
refs.explain: The title is the joined positional words; an empty title prints usage and exits 1. taskOrigin decides whether the add is allowed, and a refusal exits 2. addTask appends the task (or puts it first with --top) with the flags and origin tags merged in. save writes the store, the log gets an 'add' line, and the new id is printed with a drain hint.
refs.why: This is the entry point of the flow: the owner's request becomes a typed task with an id. Skipping it leaves the request only in chat, where no later step can find it.

refs.anchor: if (parent && !q.tasks.some(t => t.id === parent)) return { ok: false, error: `queue add: --parent ${parent} is not a task in this queue` };
refs.title: taskOrigin: refuse an agent's add without the owner's words
refs.explain: It reads the --parent and --requested flags. An unknown parent id is an error. With neither flag, it checks the environment for agent markers such as CLAUDECODE or CODEX_THREAD_ID: an agent session is refused with the AGENT_ADD_REFUSAL message, a human passes. Otherwise it returns tags and a note that record the parent or the quoted request on the task.
refs.why: This is the check behind 'only the owner creates tasks'. Without it an agent could grow the backlog with its own ideas. The comment at the top of the file notes the quote is not authenticated, so this is a guardrail, not proof.

refs.anchor: function renderView(db: DatabaseSync, defer: Defer, q: Queue, { discardEdits = false } = {}): void {
refs.title: renderView: rewrite queue.md from the store on every save
refs.explain: Unless told to discard edits, it first checks that queue.md was not hand-edited since the last render. It serializes the queue to Markdown and records the text's sha256 in the store. After the transaction commits it writes a temp file and renames it over queue.md.
refs.why: queue.db is the store and queue.md is its readable view; this keeps the two in step on each change. The rename means a reader never sees half a file, and the hash check stops a save from silently overwriting hand edits.

refs.anchor: /** A pending task is eligible only when it isn't held and every dependency is done. */
refs.title: isEligible and deadlocked: the kinds of waiting
refs.explain: isEligible is true for a pending task that is not held, is allowed by the delivery gate, and whose every dependency is done. deadlocked lists pending tasks with a dependency that failed, which can never become eligible on their own.
refs.why: These two predicates are the eligible, waiting and held states of a pending task. tick uses deadlocked to say why an idle queue is stuck.

refs.anchor: * The single task a serial worker should act on now: resume an active task if one
refs.title: nextActionable: resume the active task, else the top eligible one
refs.explain: A stopped queue returns null. Otherwise it returns the first active task the delivery gate allows; if there is none, the first eligible task in list order; else null.
refs.why: Line order in the queue is the priority, and this is where that order is applied. An already active task is always resumed before anything new starts.

refs.anchor: ? `queue: IDLE — ${stuck.length} task(s) blocked by a failed dependency: ${stuck.map(x => x.id).join(', ')}`
refs.title: queue tick: start the next task and print it
refs.explain: It runs dispatchGate and returns its exit code if blocked. It asks nextActionable for a task; with none it prints IDLE (naming tasks stuck behind a failed dependency) and exits 3. A pending task is begun, the delivery task is latched, the queue is saved, and the task block is printed with the done/fail commands. Exit 0.
refs.why: This is the serial loop's entry: one call moves the top task from pending to active. The exit codes let a driver tell 'work started' from idle, paused, stopped, conflict and delivery pending without parsing text.

refs.anchor: export function cmdClaim(q: Queue, id: string, flags: Map<string, string>, taskBlock: (t: Task) => string): number {
refs.title: queue claim: give a pending task to a worker or slot
refs.explain: refusal rejects a task that is not pending, is held, or is blocked by an unfinished delivery cycle. branchFlag rejects a --branch value that is not one name. The worker name comes from --worker, else a name built from the process id. One save marks the task active with that owner and, when given, links the branch in the same write.
refs.why: This is how a slot takes a task: the task's owner becomes the slot id. Linking the branch in the same write means a task is never active with an unlinked branch.

refs.anchor: console.log(`queue: DELIVERY PENDING — ${q.config.deliveryTask}; finish its PR/merge cycle and fresh branch, then advance`);
refs.title: dispatchGate: stop on a pause, an expired lease or a pending delivery
refs.explain: It auto-resumes a usage pause whose time has come. A stopped queue returns exit 4 (paused until a time) or 5 (stopped). Any active task older than leaseMinutes prints OWNERSHIP CONFLICT and returns 6 without touching the claim. In per-task mode, a latched delivery task with nothing actionable returns 7.
refs.why: tick and ready call this first. An expired lease stops dispatch and is reported; it is never reclaimed, because the queue cannot know whether the worker is still running.

refs.title: queue done: validate, complete, archive
refs.explain: If the task has a validate command and --skip-validate is absent, it runs it with the queue lock released, reloads the queue, and aborts if the task changed meanwhile. A failed validation records a failure and exits 1. Otherwise it marks the task done, removes every done task no unfinished task depends on, appends those to archive.md, and logs it.
refs.why: Done is decided by the validate command, not by the worker's say-so. The reload check stops a long validation from overwriting a change another process made.

refs.anchor: const tasks = terminal ? q.tasks.map(t => (t.id === id ? updated : t)) : [...rest, updated];
refs.title: recordFailure: retry until maxFailures, then failed
refs.explain: It adds one to the task's failure count and stores the reason as the note. Below maxFailures the task goes back to pending and moves to the end of the list; at maxFailures it becomes failed and keeps its place. Owner, worktree and lease are cleared and elapsed time is banked either way.
refs.why: This is the retry-or-failed branch of the outcome. Moving a retry to the back lets other work run first; a failed task stays visible until requeue or archive.

refs.anchor: * `isEligible` resolves a task's `deps` against the *live* queue, so a done task is
refs.title: archivableDone: which done tasks may leave the queue
refs.explain: It collects the ids that any pending or active task lists as a dependency. It returns the done tasks not in that set. Failed tasks are never returned.
refs.why: Dependencies are resolved against the live queue, so archiving a done task that pending work depends on would block that work forever. That is why a done task sometimes stays.

refs.title: selectDelivery and deliveryAllows: one task per delivery cycle
refs.explain: selectDelivery stores the task id in config.deliveryTask unless the mode is batch or a task is already selected. deliveryAllows answers whether a given task may start: always in batch mode; otherwise only when nothing is selected or it is the selected task.
refs.why: The selection lives in config, so it survives the task being marked done and archived. That is what holds the queue until the PR cycle is acknowledged.

refs.anchor: console.error('advance: requires selected completed task, no active claims, --pr <merged-pr-url> and --branch <fresh-working-branch>');
refs.title: queue advance: record the merged PR and the fresh branch
refs.explain: It refuses unless the id is the selected delivery task, that task was accepted as done, no task is active, --pr looks like a pull request URL and --branch is not empty. On success it clears deliveryTask and deliveryAccepted, saves, and writes the PR and branch to the log.
refs.why: This closes the delivery cycle so the queue will hand out the next task. The code checks only the queue's own state and the URL's shape; it does not ask GitHub whether the PR merged, so the orchestrator vouches for that.

refs.title: Test: tick exits 7 until advance is given a PR and a branch
refs.explain: With two tasks, tick starts the first and claim or begin on the second is refused. After done, tick and ready exit 7 and signal exits 3. advance fails for the wrong task and without --pr/--branch, then succeeds, and the next tick starts the second task.
refs.why: It pins the rule that a done task still holds the queue and that exit 7 means delivery pending, not drained.
